extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, and mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for understanding, teaching, and assessing mathematical problem solving, including knowledge inventories, heuristics (Pólya-style), memory/processing constraints, classroom implementation, and self-regulation/metacognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The knowledge inventory (memory contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects of the knowledge base relevant for competent performance in a domain include: informal and intuitive knowledge about the domain; facts, definitions, and the like; algorithmic procedures; routine procedures; relevant competencies; and knowledge about the rules of discourse in the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example context: constructing a circle tangent to two lines with a specified tangency point — informal intuitions about tangency, perceptual biases (symmetry), and formal constraints must be exploited within construction rules. Note that items in the inventory may be incorrect (misconceptions) yet still be the tools students use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of knowledge / certainty about facts and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals vary in whether they (a) know nothing, (b) know of existence only, (c) partially recall/suspect details with little certainty, or (d) confidently believe a fact or procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 examples: correct procedure for bisecting an angle, correct procedure for dropping a perpendicular, incorrect belief that center of inscribed circle lies at intersection of medians. Instruction and assessment should note not just correctness but degree of certainty and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine procedures and relevant competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine procedures and competencies are less cut-and-dried than facts/algorithms: they are likely to work but have no formal guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For construction problems linked to proofs, relevant proof techniques (e.g., seeking congruent triangles, drawing segments CV/CP/CQ, using SSS/ASA/AAS/hypotenuse-leg) are routine methods that should drive the search process. Evaluate whether students activate appropriate routine proof methods and know which components to draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the rules of discourse in the domain (formal constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge about what actions are permitted in the formal game (e.g., Euclidean geometry constructions) — the domain's procedural constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of proscribed actions: 'lining up' a tangent by eye, determining a diameter by sliding a ruler to find the largest chord. Students who grasp these rules will behave differently from those who don't; assessment should check adherence to formal allowable methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to resources / structure of memory
rubrics_metrics.description: How memory contents are organized, accessed, and processed (sensory buffer → working memory → long-term memory) matters for problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 framework: stimuli (visual/auditory/tactile) → sensory buffer → working memory (where thinking gets done) and long-term memory. Instructional tasks should consider how information is encoded and retrieved; designers should scaffold retrieval from LTM into working memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working memory limits and chunking (working memory load)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working/short-term memory has limited capacity (Miller's ~7±2 chunks), which constrains the amount and kind of mental processing possible during problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chunks can be complex (e.g., words, ideograms, board configurations), so instruction should aim to build useful chunks and reduce working memory load. Problems requiring many intermediate subtotals (e.g., mental multiplication of 637 and 829) illustrate STM limits; design and assessment should account for chunking ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of long-term memory: chunks, schemata, scripts, frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term memory is organized as networks of chunks (scripts/frames/schemata) whose links represent connections; expertise depends on having large vocabularies of recognizable configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: de Groot/chess analogy: experts recognize ~50,000 configurations. In mathematics, well-developed chunks enable rapid response but overreliance may lead to surface performance. Instruction should foster rich and connected LTM representations, not only rote pattern recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarative vs procedural knowledge (knowing that vs knowing how)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction exists between declarative ('knowing that') and procedural ('knowing how') knowledge; both are important and their relationship is complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and assessment should probe both types and their interplay (e.g., whether a student can articulate facts and also apply procedures), recognizing that neither alone suffices for robust problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya-style heuristics / problem-solving strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic strategies such as analogy, auxiliary elements, decomposing and recombining, induction, specialization, variation, and working backwards are central problem-solving resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Pólya's heuristics have face validity, early formulations were descriptive rather than prescriptive. Effective teaching needs to render these heuristics implementable (fine-grained, context-specific guidance) rather than merely naming them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and use of special cases as a heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining special cases can clarify unfamiliar problems, but the 'right' special cases depend on problem type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for integer-parameter problems examine n=1,2,3,... to see a pattern; for polynomial-root relationships consider easily factorable polynomials; for recursively defined sequences try initial values like 0 and 1 if they preserve generality. Teaching must guide students to pick fruitful special cases rather than generic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescriptive characterization and teaching of heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics can be taught effectively if characterized at a fine-grained, prescriptive level and supported by explicit methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations (Heller & Hungate): (a) make tacit processes explicit, (b) get students talking about processes, (c) provide guided practice, (d) ensure component procedures are well learned, (e) emphasize both qualitative understanding and specific procedures. AI/education parallels (Rissland, Newell) support detailed, learnable strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of problem solving in curricula vs superficial inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem solving is often presented superficially in curricula (occasional 'problem solving' items or separate sections), which conveys that problem solving is an occasional pastime rather than central mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common textbook practice: 'exposition, examples, exercises' mode and isolated problem-solving sections that turn heuristics into rote algorithms. Curriculum design should integrate investigative tasks and authentic problem contexts rather than treating problem solving as optional or purely procedural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding crude schema-focused instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying solely on crude schemata ('when you see these features, use this procedure') risks producing surface-level competence that is error-prone and easily forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educators should ensure schemata are grounded in underlying principles; emphasize understanding why procedures work and when they fail, not only pattern-triggered procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher demands for effective problem solving instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching problem solving is more demanding on teachers mathematically, pedagogically, and personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burkhardt's summary: teachers must (mathematically) perceive implications of diverse student approaches, (pedagogically) decide when/how to intervene while leaving solution ownership to students, and (personally) be comfortable not knowing all answers. Professional development should target these areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation (monitoring and control) during problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-regulation entails resource allocation during cognitive activity: planning, monitoring, and evaluation — assessing on-line progress and acting accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rereading when understanding is fuzzy, revising writing when off-outline, restarting a complex problem when initial approach is inadequate. Instruction should foster explicit monitoring strategies and decision rules for when to continue, revise, or abandon an approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental progression of self-regulation skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-regulatory planning and corrective judgment abilities tend to improve with age; younger children often act without systematic planning while older children plan and sort resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Karmiloff-Smith track-building study: 4-5 year olds jump in randomly; 8-9 year olds sort pieces and follow systematic plans. Assessment and instruction should be age-appropriate and scaffold planning behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive control and opportunistic planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective problem solving requires executive control that may be opportunistic (local decisions suggesting opportunities) rather than strictly top-down hierarchical planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI models: NOAH (top-down), bottom-up models, Hayes-Roth's Opportunistic Planning Model (OPM). In practice planners act opportunistically, refocusing when new observations suggest alternative plans. Teaching should cultivate flexible planning and the ability to refocus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not just knowledge but appropriate use of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Competent problem solving depends not only on what is known but on how, when, and whether that knowledge is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies show many solution attempts involve quickly choosing an approach and persisting despite lack of progress (read→decide→pursue). Instruction should target monitoring and conditional use of knowledge to avoid sinkhole persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation and analytic behavior in problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of time use distinguish novice behavior (quick choice, persistent pursuit with little analysis) from expert behavior (extended sense-making, exploration, and planning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 3 and 4 contrast typical student attempts (read→choose quickly→implement with little analysis) versus mathematician attempts (spend over half the time making sense, exploring multiple directions). Assessment should examine time-use patterns and encourage extended analysis phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional goal: developing executive/control skills through extended practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses and instructional sequences can have as a major goal the development of executive or control skills (planning, monitoring, revising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schoenfeld's problem solving courses use extensive videotape analyses and structured activities to train students to monitor and regulate their approaches. Effective programs allocate significant time to reflection, feedback, and practice in control behaviors.
